https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: The Centre on Friday informed the Supreme Court that two Indian seafarers who went missing after their cargo vessel was attacked in the Black Sea near Ukraine remain untraceable despite extensive search and rescue operations involving Ukrainian and Romanian authorities.Appearing before a bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said the search efforts were carried out by Ukrainian authorities, the Romanian Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC), the Romanian Coast Guard and other rescue agencies, but had failed to locate the missing crew members.Also Read: Surge in Black Sea attacks adds to strain on global commodity flowsTaking note of the Action Taken Report (ATR) filed jointly by the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) and the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA), the bench recorded that, based on information available until August 5, the two missing seafarers — Deepak Kumar Gupta and Rama Chandra — could not be found despite exhaustive efforts. It is stated that search operations presently remain suspended pending receipt of fresh information while DGMA continues to pursue all pending investigation and SAR (search and rescue operations) reports and remains engaged with all concerned stakeholders , the court said in its order.The bench also directed the Centre to facilitate insurance claims for the families of the missing seafarers, noting that the employment contracts provided insurance cover.The court was hearing a petition filed by Sandeep Kumar Gupta, elder brother of 22-year-old Deepak Kumar Gupta, seeking directions to the MEA to coordinate with the Indian embassies in Ukraine and Romania to ensure effective search and rescue operations.The petition said the family approached the MEA and the Indian missions in both countries between July 26 and July 30, but their repeated representations neither received a response nor any concrete assurance.Also Read: India urges caution for ships entering Black SeaAt the outset of the hearing, Mehta told the court that the MEA and DGMA had jointly filed the status report and that, despite their best efforts, the two missing Indians could not be traced.Justice Bagchi observed that since the seafarers' employment contracts included insurance provisions, the government should assist their families in securing the claims.Counsel appearing for the families, however, alleged that no meaningful search and rescue operation had been undertaken, contending that the Indian embassy's publicly available information reflected the situation only up to July 26.Responding to the allegation, Mehta said there was no practical purpose in continuing search operations at sea at this stage, but assured the court that the authorities remained in constant touch with all concerned stakeholders and were continuing to monitor developments.On August 3, the Supreme Court had directed the MEA to use diplomatic channels to trace the missing seafarers. It had asked Mehta to obtain instructions from the Indian Embassy in Ukraine and the Embassy of India in Bucharest, Romania, regarding Deepak Gupta's whereabouts.According to the petition, Deepak Gupta, a resident of Bharataul village in Uttar Pradesh's Bareilly district, was serving as a crew member aboard the merchant vessel MV AGN Ragnar when it came under attack near Ukraine's Odesa port.Though his family originally belongs to Bihar's Siwan district, they have been living in Bharataul village for several years.

https://www.baltictimes.com/russian_mili.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Russian military has not become weaker - Rinkevics 2026-09-10 LETA/TBT Staff Photo: LETA RIGA - The Russian military has not grown weaker and is completely different from what it was four and a half years ago, President Edgars Rinkevics emphasized Thursday at the opening of the Riga Conference. He stressed that Russia’s military forces must not be underestimated simply because the war imposes economic costs on the country, and Russian society is increasingly coming to realize what that means. "Let’s not be misled into thinking that this means a weakening of Russia’s military capabilities. Quite the opposite. We must understand that Russia’s military forces are, in fact, well-developed," said Rinkevics. Compared to last year, the President sees several positive changes; for example, Ukraine has been able to withstand the pressure, launch counterattacks, and make the Russian public bear some of the costs of the war. Rinkevics emphasized that there is constant competition in the field of military technology - drone warfare, anti-drone defenses, ballistic missiles, and their interception systems are all evolving. In his view, although Ukraine has made significant progress in this area, similar technological developments are also taking place in Russia. The President is convinced that Ukrainian society and political leadership have the will to continue the fight; however, Ukraine still needs comprehensive political, moral, and practical support. He explained that this applies to military equipment, ballistic missile interceptors and related systems, as well as anti-drone defense capabilities. Rinkevics stated that Ukraine also needs financial support so that it can continue the fight and the country can function. The President commended the European Union’s (EU) ability to provide Ukraine with EUR 90 billion in funding, as well as NATO’s PURL initiative. He emphasized that promises alone are not enough and that the agreements reached must also be implemented by providing actual funding. The President called for continued efforts to increase political and economic pressure on Russia and to agree on stricter sanctions. He acknowledged that the current sanctions regime is complicated, as it contains many exceptions and nuances, and therefore a unified European approach is needed. Rinkevics emphasized that Latvia’s position on the issue of frozen Russian assets has always been clear: namely, they must be used to support Ukraine. He acknowledged that reaching an agreement among all 27 EU member states on this issue is not easy. The President stressed that EU member states must jointly shoulder both the responsibility and the costs. In his view, it is unacceptable for one country to bear the full brunt of the pressure exerted by Russia, while other EU member states stand on the sidelines and simply wish good luck to countries that might face Russian pressure. Turning to regional security, the President emphasized that there is currently no observable concentration of Russian conventional military forces near the borders of the Baltic states or other NATO member states; however, this year’s security situation differs significantly from that of 2021 due to technological advancements. The President acknowledged that various provocations are possible that could cause worry, but would most likely not reach the threshold for invoking Article 5 of the NATO Treaty, forcing the allies to seek an appropriate response. Rinkevics mentioned the increasing intensity of unconventional warfare. The President emphasized that the number of cyberattacks and acts of sabotage is increasing and that residents of Latvia and other NATO and EU countries are being involved in such activities. Various espionage activities also continue. The President noted that a coordinated response can halt Russia’s provocations. He referred to NATO’s Operation Baltic Sentry in connection with incidents involving undersea cables and Operation Eastern Sentry following airspace violations in NATO countries. Rinkevics said that following the measures taken, the number of such incidents has decreased. He noted that this does not mean similar incidents cannot recur, but the measures taken by the allies have yielded results. The President called for a reevaluation of the use of the term "hybrid war", as it can create a misleading impression among the public regarding the apparent harmlessness of such attacks. He called on NATO and the EU to seek new solutions for responding to sabotage, cyberattacks, espionage, and other provocations that do not reach the level of a conventional military attack. The President also addressed defense spending. Rinkevics emphasized that allocating five percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to defense spending is necessary to enhance the security of NATO allies and strengthen their defenses. He acknowledged that even five percent of GDP might not be enough. Rinkevics called for defense planning to take new trends in warfare more fully into account, without neglecting conventional military capabilities.
